paper_context.research_question: Can fully automatic, knowledge-base-mined annotations from Wikipedia and related KB properties be used to build accurate cross-lingual name tagging, fine/coarse-grained typing, and linking systems for a very large set of languages (282), without manual annotation or native-speaker input?
contribution_type: resource/benchmark (silver-standard annotations, morphology analyzers, systems for 282 languages)
empirical evaluation (large-scale experiments on Wikipedia and non-Wikipedia corpora)
contribution_style: integrated system description (pipeline combining multiple modules)
data mining methods (KB-derived features, cross-lingual transfer, word-translation mining)
experimental benchmarking (performance tables across 282 languages and Non-Wikipedia tests)
main_claims: A fully automatic pipeline that mines Wikipedia markups and KB properties can produce useful "silver-standard" name annotations and train name taggers for 282 languages without manual labels or native-speaker input.
Leveraging DBpedia/YAGO properties and AMR-to-YAGO mappings yields multi-granularity entity typing that generalizes across languages.
Self-training and cross-lingual topic selection substantially improve coverage and accuracy of automatically generated annotations.
Morphology features derived from Wikipedia markups (affix lists) improve name tagging for morphologically rich languages (e.g., Turkish, Uzbek).
Mining word translation pairs from cross-lingual Wikipedia title pairs allows effective cross-lingual name translation and unsupervised linking to an English KB.

On Wikipedia-derived test data the framework attains high tagging F-scores (> ~80%) and linking accuracy (> ~80%) for many languages; on external news/forum datasets the silver-trained models approach supervised gold-trained models (within ~5.8–17.6% absolute F-score gap) and outperform some prior language-independent baselines.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Name tagging accuracy (precision/recall/F-score) broken down by language and entity type (PER/ORG/GPE/LOC and finer-grained types).
Entity linking accuracy for linkable mentions (precision/accuracy of KB disambiguation).
Robustness/generalization: performance on non-Wikipedia corpora (news, forums) vs. Wikipedia-derived test sets.
Resource coverage: number of languages supported (282) and quantity/quality of silver-standard annotations per language.
Ablation analyses: contribution of components (KB-property typing, self-training, morphology features, translation mining) to final performance.
Sensitivity to resource sparsity: performance as a function of number of linked mentions per language.
Error analysis: common failure modes (scripts without spaces, low-mention languages, transliteration/translation failures).

extracted_claims.claim_text: A fully automatic pipeline that mines Wikipedia markups and KB properties (DBpedia/YAGO) can produce useful silver-standard name annotations and train name taggers for 282 languages without manual labels or native-speaker input.
evidence: Abstract: describes a fully automatic pipeline for 282 languages without manual labels or native-speaker input.
Introduction: states leveraging Wikipedia markups for a cross-lingual name tagging and linking system for 282 languages.
Section 2.2: details classifying English pages using AMR+KB properties and propagating labels via cross-lingual links.
Conclusions: reiterates fully automatic training and testing pipeline and release of resources for 282 languages.
uncertainty_flags: The term 'useful' is not precisely defined with consistent downstream thresholds.
Quality and coverage vary greatly across languages depending on number of mentions and KB coverage.
Relies on presence and correctness of cross-lingual links and KB properties for many languages.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Leveraging AMR annotations and mappings to the YAGO type hierarchy together with DBpedia/YAGO properties yields multi-granularity entity typing that generalizes across languages.
evidence: Section 2.2: uses AMR corpus types mapped to YAGO to produce three levels of typing (4 coarse types, 139 AMR types, 9,154 YAGO types).
Section 2.2: describes using DBpedia properties as features to train classifiers for assigning types.
uncertainty_flags: Mapping quality depends on PMI computed from a relatively small AMR corpus (2,756 mentions), which may introduce noise.
Generalization across languages assumes accurate cross-lingual links connecting equivalent pages.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Using entity properties from DBpedia as features eliminates the need for language-specific features/resources (e.g., POS tags) when classifying English KB pages and propagating types cross-lingually.
evidence: Section 2.2: explicitly states exploiting DBpedia properties as features to avoid language-specific resources.
Table 1: lists KB-derived features (e.g., gazetteer, embeddings, entity properties).
uncertainty_flags: DBpedia coverage and consistency vary by entity and language; sparse or noisy properties will propagate errors.
The approach reduces English-side language features but assumes cross-lingual propagation preserves validity in target languages.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Self-training (iterative bootstrapping with NPMI-based seed selection and cluster-wise addition of high-confidence predictions) substantially refines and increases coverage of automatically generated annotations.
evidence: Section 2.3: describes NPMI(seed) selection, clustering unlabeled sentences, iterative labeling and retraining.
Section 4.3: Turkish learning curves show self-training yields a 6% absolute gain on Wikipedia and 12% on Non-Wikipedia.
uncertainty_flags: Improvement examples are primarily demonstrated on Turkish; cross-language generality is not fully quantified.
Self-training can amplify errors if initial seeds or confidence estimates are noisy.

extracted_claims.claim_label: training data selection via commonness and topicality
extracted_claims.claim_text: Cross-lingual topic transfer and ranking by entity commonness and topical relatedness allow selection of high-quality annotated sentences for training, useful for rapid adaptation in scenarios like disasters.
evidence: Section 2.4: describes dynamic frequency thresholding for commonness and topical relatedness using English tagger+linker on Leidos corpus to select top Wikipedia categories.
uncertainty_flags: Empirical gains from this selection across languages/tasks are not reported numerically beyond the described procedure.
Topical selection depends on English resources and assumes topical categories transfer well to target languages.

extracted_claims.claim_label: morphology from Wiki markups improves performance
extracted_claims.claim_text: Deriving affix lists and stemming heuristics from Wikipedia markups provides morphology features that improve name tagging for morphologically rich languages (e.g., Turkish, Uzbek).
evidence: Section 2.5: explains extracting suffixes from bracketed anchor forms and using them as features for stemming and type prediction.
Section 4.2: reports morphology features contributed 11.1% and 7.1% absolute F-score gains for Turkish and Uzbek respectively.
uncertainty_flags: Method applies only when stems and affixes are concatenated; non-concatenative morphology or languages without clear tokenization are not addressed.
Reported gains are shown for two languages; broader applicability is not fully evaluated.

extracted_claims.claim_label: mining word translations from title pairs
extracted_claims.claim_text: Mining word translation pairs from cross-lingual Wikipedia title pairs via exhaustive sub-span extraction and GIZA++ alignment produces useful translation pairs that enable name translation for linking.
evidence: Section 3.2: describes generating all continuous token combinations from titles and running GIZA++ to extract word translations.
Table 2: provides examples of mined word translation pairs with alignment confidences.
uncertainty_flags: Coverage is limited; only a small percentage of mentions are exact title matches, and overall coverage numbers are not provided.
Alignments from short title pairs can be noisy, affecting translation quality.

extracted_claims.claim_text: An unsupervised collective inference approach that constructs knowledge networks from context and compares salience/similarity/coherence with KB candidate networks can link translated mentions to English DBpedia with high accuracy for linkable mentions.
evidence: Section 3.3: describes constructing KNs g(ti) and g(ej), candidate retrieval via surface-form dictionary, and scoring based on salience, similarity, and coherence.
Section 4.1 / Table 3: reports linking accuracy higher than 80% for many languages on Wikipedia-derived linkable mentions.
uncertainty_flags: Linking accuracy is computed only for mentions deemed linkable; unlinkable detection and end-to-end recall are not fully reported.
Candidate generation coverage and common failure cases (e.g., NIL handling) are not thoroughly detailed.

extracted_claims.claim_text: On Wikipedia-derived test data the framework attains high tagging F-scores (> ~80%) and linking accuracy (> ~80%) for many languages, with performance strongly correlated with number of mentions per language (e.g., >30K mentions usually >80% F-score).
evidence: Section 4.1: notes F-score generally >80% when >30K mentions, and drops when mentions <250.
Table 3: provides per-language mentions, F-scores, and linking accuracies across many languages.
uncertainty_flags: Evaluation uses silver-standard test data derived from the same pipeline, so high scores may reflect consistency with noisy labels rather than absolute quality versus human gold annotations.
Large per-language variability indicates thresholds where performance degrades sharply.

extracted_claims.claim_text: On external news/forum (Non-Wikipedia) datasets in nine languages, models trained on silver-standard annotations achieve performance that approaches supervised gold-trained models, with absolute F-score gaps of ~5.8–17.6%, and outperform some prior language-independent baselines.
evidence: Section 4.2: compares silver-trained models to gold-trained supervised models and language-independent baselines, reporting 5.8%–17.6% lower F-scores than gold-trained models.
Tables 4 and 5: show dataset sizes and per-language F-scores on Non-Wikipedia test data.
uncertainty_flags: Comparison covers nine languages only (LORELEI selection), which may bias representativeness.
Some baseline comparisons have missing entries; direct comparability is not uniform.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Cross-lingual Wikipedia interlanguage links reliably connect equivalent entity pages across languages.
supporting_evidence: Section 2.2: propagates English page labels to other languages via cross-lingual links.
Section 3.2: mines translation pairs from cross-lingual title pairs.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Missing or incorrect interlanguage links will cause incorrect or incomplete propagated types and translations, degrading tagging and linking quality, especially in low-resource languages.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: DBpedia/YAGO properties for an entity are accurate, sufficiently populated, and discriminative for entity typing.
supporting_evidence: Section 2.2: uses properties like birthDate or population as features for Maximum Entropy classifiers.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Noisy or sparse KB properties will lead to misclassification of English KB pages and propagate label noise across languages.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: AMR corpus mappings (2,756 mentions) provide sufficient signal to map AMR types to YAGO types and build multi-granularity typing.
supporting_evidence: Section 2.2: computes PMI between AMR and YAGO types using AMR mentions.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Small AMR sample size could yield unreliable PMI estimates and noisy type mappings, degrading fine-grained typing quality.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: NPMI-based seed selection and clustering reliably identify clean seed sentences for self-training across many languages.
supporting_evidence: Section 2.3: uses NPMI(tag, token) > τ with τ=0 and clustering (n=20) to select seeds for iterative self-training.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Poor separation by NPMI or ineffective clustering in low-resource or noisy languages can lead self-training to amplify errors rather than improve coverage.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Affixes learned from bracketed anchor markups reflect true morphological affixes and generalize beyond anchor occurrences.
supporting_evidence: Section 2.5: extracts suffixes (e.g., Turkish 'den', 'ne') from anchor-marked examples and uses them as features.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Extraction may conflate clitics, postpositions, or orthographic artifacts with morphological affixes, misleading stemming and type prediction in affected languages.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Word translation pairs mined from title pairs via GIZA++ are of sufficient quality to support name translation for linking.
supporting_evidence: Section 3.2: describes exhaustive sub-span extraction and GIZA++ alignment; Table 2 shows extracted pairs with confidence scores.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Noisy alignments from short or sparse title pairs may produce incorrect translations, harming candidate generation and linking accuracy.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Training and test splits from silver-standard Wikipedia annotations provide valid within-domain evaluation of model predictability.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.1: uses a 70/30 split of selected Wikipedia sentences for training/testing and reports F-scores and linking accuracy.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: High scores on silver-standard test data may overestimate real-world performance because train and test share annotation noise and heuristics.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Linking accuracy computed only on mentions with candidate surface-form matches is representative of overall linking performance.
supporting_evidence: Section 3.3: candidate entities are generated from a surface-form dictionary; Section 4.1: linking accuracy computed for linkable mentions only.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Excluding unlinkable mentions hides recall failures and end-to-end coverage; reported linking accuracy may not reflect overall system utility.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Performance on nine Non-Wikipedia LORELEI languages generalizes to other non-Wikipedia, low-resource domains.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.2: evaluates on nine languages using Leidos/LORELEI datasets and compares to gold-trained models and baselines.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: The selected nine languages may not be representative; generalization to other domains or languages with different scripts/tokenization is uncertain.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: BiLSTM+CRF model architecture trained on silver data generalizes across typologically diverse languages, including those without spaces.
supporting_evidence: Section 2.3: uses BiLSTM+CRF as the underlying model; Section 4.1: notes lower performance for languages without spaces (Chinese, Thai, Japanese).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Model performance may degrade on languages with different tokenization/orthography unless special preprocessing is applied; current results show limitations.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues that Wikipedia markups combined with KB properties (DBpedia/YAGO) can automatically produce large-scale silver-standard name annotations and train taggers/linkers for 282 languages without manual or native-speaker input. The pipeline: (1) classify English Wikipedia pages into multi-granularity types using AMR→YAGO mappings and DBpedia properties; (2) propagate labels via cross-lingual links; (3) expand/clean annotations via NPMI seed selection + iterative self-training; (4) select topical/common training data when needed; (5) derive morphology features from bracketed anchors; (6) mine word translations from cross-lingual title pairs using exhaustive sub-span extraction + GIZA++; (7) translate mentions and apply an unsupervised collective linker using knowledge-network similarity. Empirical evidence: large-scale silver-splits (70/30) show tagging F-scores and linking accuracy often >80% on Wikipedia-derived test data (Table 3), morphology features show large gains for Turkish/Uzbek, self-training improves Turkish by 6–12% absolute, and evaluation on nine non-Wikipedia languages shows silver-trained models are within ~5.8–17.6% absolute F-score of gold-trained models and outperform some language-independent baselines. Key risks: many evaluations are on silver-standard data (shared noise between train/test), several modules rely on sparse supervision (AMR corpus has only 2,756 mentions), interlanguage links and DBpedia properties are assumed to be broadly reliable, and linking accuracy is reported only for 'linkable' mentions, hiding end-to-end recall/NIL rates. Overall, the paper presents a coherent, end-to-end engineering pipeline with extensive breadth; its argument hinges on the quality and coverage of KB signals and cross-lingual links and on whether silver-standard performance generalizes to gold-standard, out-of-domain settings.
logical_argument_graph: P0: Task statement — need multilingual name tagging/linking across many languages without human annotation.

C1 -> P1: English pages can be typed into multi-granular schemas by mapping AMR types to YAGO and training classifiers using DBpedia properties (AMR provides labeled seed; DBpedia properties are language-independent features).
P1 -> C2: Propagate English page labels via cross-lingual links to produce initial silver-standard annotations across languages (anchor links and redirects yield training mentions).

C2 -> P2: These initial annotations are incomplete (only first anchor, surface-form mismatches) => apply self-training with NPMI-based seed selection and cluster-wise iterative labeling to expand coverage.
P2 -> C3: For populous languages, ranking by entity commonness and topical relatedness yields high-quality selected training sets for rapid adaptation (e.g., disaster scenarios).
P1 & P2 -> C4: Extract morphology (stems/affixes) from bracketed anchors to generate language-specific morphology features that improve tagging for morphologically rich languages.

P1 & external resources -> C5: Mine word/phrase translation pairs from cross-lingual Wikipedia title pairs using exhaustive sub-spans + alignment (GIZA++) to enable translation of mentions for linking.
C5 -> P3: Translate mentions into English and do unsupervised collective linking by building knowledge networks for mentions and candidate KB entities and scoring by salience/similarity/coherence.

Empirical evidence node (E): Wikipedia 70/30 experiments show high F and linking accuracy correlated with mention counts; Non-Wikipedia evaluations (9 languages) show silver-trained models approach gold-trained baselines within reported gaps; morphology and self-training ablations reported for specific languages (Turkish, Uzbek).
Conclusion node: The pipeline yields useful silver-standard annotations and functioning tagger/linker systems across 282 languages, with resource releases.

Implicit dependency edges / failure modes: reliability of cross-lingual links, DBpedia property coverage, small AMR mapping sample, GIZA++ noise from short title pairs, evaluation bias from silver-standard test sets, unlinkable mention coverage not reported.

strengths.title: Comprehensive end-to-end pipeline at unprecedented language scale
strengths.description: The paper describes a full engineering pipeline from KB mining to tagger and linker applied to 282 languages and releases the resulting resources, which is a significant engineering and resource contribution.
evidence: Introduction and Conclusions: claim of 282 languages and resource release.
Sections 2-3: detailed pipeline components (typing, propagation, self-training, morphology, translation, linking).
Table 3: shows per-language metrics across hundreds of languages.

strengths.title: Novel use of KB properties and AMR→YAGO mapping for multi-granular typing
strengths.description: Combining AMR-labeled mentions with PMI mapping to YAGO and DBpedia properties to produce three-granularity type labels is an explicit attempt to build cross-lingual, KB-driven typing without language-specific NLP.
evidence: Section 2.2: AMR to YAGO PMI mapping and use of DBpedia properties as classifier features.
Claims of 10M English pages labeled and three granularity levels (4 coarse, 139 AMR, 9,154 YAGO).

strengths.title: Targeted morphology extraction from anchor markups
strengths.description: The method to extract affixes/stems from bracketed anchor forms is a low-cost way to obtain morphological cues from data already present in Wikipedia.
evidence: Section 2.5: example Turkish sentence and suffix extraction explanation.
Section 4.2: reported +11.1% and +7.1% absolute F-score gains for Turkish and Uzbek respectively.

strengths.title: Practical translation mining using title sub-spans
strengths.description: Exhaustive sub-span extraction of title pairs followed by alignment (GIZA++) is a pragmatic approach to obtain translation pairs for names and phrases without parallel corpora.
evidence: Section 3.2: exhaustive combinations and GIZA++ pipeline.
Table 2: example mined translations with confidence scores.

concerns.title: Evaluation relies heavily on silver-standard test data
concerns.description: Most performance numbers (Table 3) are computed on test splits drawn from the same automatically labeled Wikipedia data generation procedure; this risks conflating consistency with the pipeline's heuristics and noise with true accuracy against human gold labels.
evidence: Section 4.1: 70/30 split of selected Wikipedia sentences (silver-standard) for train/test; explicit note that results estimate predictability of silver data but are not directly comparable to human-annotated gold data.
Large per-language variability and dependence on number of mentions indicate pipeline-specific effects.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add targeted human evaluation (span-level, type-level, linking correctness) on a stratified sample across language families, scripts (space-less vs spaced), and mention-count buckets; report precision/recall against human gold for a representative subset (e.g., 20 diverse languages).

concerns.title: AMR→YAGO mapping is underpowered and potentially noisy
concerns.description: The mapping from AMR types to thousands of YAGO types is computed from only 2,756 AMR mentions; PMI estimates at this sample size may be noisy and could inject systematic fine-type errors that propagate across languages.
evidence: Section 2.2: AMR corpus size = 2,756 mentions used to compute PMI.
Claim of producing 9,154 YAGO types mapped from AMR despite small mapping sample.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report sample mappings and precision estimates (precision@k) for AMR→YAGO mappings; consider thresholding or human spot-checking of high-frequency mappings and performing ablation to show sensitivity of downstream typing to mapping noise.

concerns.title: Linking evaluation omits unlinkable mentions and end-to-end recall
concerns.description: Linking accuracy is computed only for mentions deemed 'linkable' (surface-form matches), leaving end-to-end linking coverage and NIL detection performance unreported. This masks the system's practical utility.
evidence: Section 4.1: explicit statement 'we only compute linking accuracy for linkable name mentions.'
Section 3.3: candidate generation depends on surface-form dictionary from KB properties.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report end-to-end linking metrics: mention detection→translation→candidate generation coverage, overall precision/recall/F1 including NIL assignment, and per-language candidate generation coverage statistics.

concerns.title: Uneven cross-lingual propagation assumptions (interlanguage link reliability)
concerns.description: The approach assumes cross-lingual interlanguage links accurately connect equivalent entity pages across languages; in low-resource or noisy Wikipedias, links can be missing or incorrect, which would propagate wrong types/translations.
evidence: Sections 2.2 and 3.2: propagation and translation mining rely on cross-lingual links and title pairs.
Identified assumption A1 in shared analysis: missing/incorrect links degrade quality.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide empirical statistics on interlanguage link coverage and precision for a stratified set of low-, mid-, and high-resource Wikipedias; include fallback heuristics or confidence scores when links are sparse or contradictory.

concerns.title: Self-training generality not established
concerns.description: Self-training improvements are demonstrated mainly with detailed results for Turkish; cross-language generality and robustness to seed noise are not quantified, raising the possibility of error amplification in many languages.
evidence: Section 4.3: Turkish learning curves and gains reported; Section 2.3 describes NPMI seeds with τ=0, clusters n=20.
Shared analysis notes self-training risk if seeds/confidences are noisy.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report ablation across a representative set of languages (including low-mention and non-Latin-script languages) comparing with and without self-training, and measure label-flip rates or noise amplification across iterations.

concerns.title: Translation mining coverage and noise unclear
concerns.description: While examples of mined translation pairs are shown, the manuscript does not quantify the coverage (fraction of mentions that can be translated) nor the precision of the mined lexicon, especially for low-resource languages or titles with abbreviations/diacritics.
evidence: Section 3.2 and Table 2 provide examples but no overall coverage/precision statistics.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper presents an end-to-end, fully automatic pipeline that mines English KB resources (AMR, DBpedia/YAGO) and Wikipedia markups to produce "silver-standard" name span, type (coarse and fine-grained) and link annotations and then trains BiLSTM-CRF taggers and an unsupervised collective linker for 282 Wikipedia languages. Key modules: (1) English-side typing via AMR-to-YAGO mapping and Maximum Entropy classifiers using DBpedia properties; (2) cross-lingual propagation via interlanguage links and redirects; (3) self-training with NPMI-based seed selection and cluster-iterative labeling; (4) topical/commonness-based training-data selection; (5) morphology features derived from anchor markups; (6) mining word translations from cross-lingual title pairs using exhaustive subspan extraction + GIZA++; (7) unsupervised collective linking using knowledge networks and salience/similarity/coherence scores. Evaluation: within-Wikipedia 70/30 splits across 282 languages (reporting tagging F and linking accuracy on linkable mentions) and out-of-domain Non-Wikipedia comparisons on nine LORELEI languages. The reported strengths include broad coverage (282 languages), competitive non-gold performance (silver-trained models within ~5.8–17.6% of gold models on nine languages), morphology gains for Turkish/Uzbek, and linking accuracy often >80% for linkable mentions. Major methodological dependencies that must hold for claims: reliability of interlanguage links, sufficiency and accuracy of DBpedia/YAGO properties, quality of AMR->YAGO mappings from a small AMR corpus, translation coverage and quality from title-pair alignment, and that silver test splits reflect true generalization. Evidence gaps and reproducibility issues center on per-language KB property coverage, noise rates in silver labels, candidate generation/linking recall (including NIL/unlinkable handling), broader cross-language validation of self-training and morphology gains, and public release of code/data to reproduce large-scale mining and alignments.
logical_argument_graph: A1: English AMR provides fine-grained type annotations -> compute PMI between AMR types and YAGO types -> produce multi-granular typing schema
A2: DBpedia/YAGO properties for entities are discriminative -> train MaxEnt classifiers to label English Wikipedia pages with types
A3: Cross-lingual interlanguage links correctly map equivalent pages -> propagate English page labels to mentions in 282 languages
A4: Propagated anchor mentions + NPMI-selected seeds -> train initial BiLSTM-CRF tagger per language
A5: Clustered self-training (NPMI seeds + iterative retraining) -> increases annotation coverage and improves tagger performance
A6: Extracted affix lists from anchor markups -> provide stemming/affix features that improve tagging on morphologically rich languages
A7: Exhaustive sub-span extraction of title pairs + GIZA++ -> produce word translation pairs used to translate mentions to English
A8: Surface-form candidate generation + knowledge network construction + salience/similarity/coherence scoring -> unsupervised linking of translated mentions to DBpedia
A9: Evaluation on silver 70/30 splits shows high within-domain predictability; out-of-domain (9 languages) shows silver-trained models approach supervised gold models within 5.8–17.6% F

Conclusion: Fully automatic, KB-mined pipeline yields usable silver-standard annotations and systems across hundreds of languages, with measurable benefits from KB features, self-training, morphology extraction, and mined translations

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that large-scale, fully automatic mining of Wikipedia markups plus KB properties (DBpedia/YAGO) can produce usable "silver-standard" annotations and train name-tagging, fine/granular typing, morphology, and cross-lingual linking systems for 282 languages without manual labeling or native-speaker input. The pipeline's reasoning chain: (1) map AMR fine-grained types to YAGO types using PMI scores computed from the AMR corpus to create a multi-granularity typing scheme; (2) train English-page classifiers using DBpedia/YAGO properties (birthDate, population, etc.) as language-independent features and propagate labels via interlanguage redirects/links to generate initial anchor-based silver annotations in many languages; (3) expand and clean these initial annotations with self-training driven by NPMI-based seed selection and clusterwise iterative labeling; (4) rank/select training sentences for rapid adaptation using entity commonness and topicality derived from English corpora; (5) derive morphology/affix features from anchor-markup bracketed forms to help morphologically-rich languages; (6) mine word/phrase translation pairs by exhaustively extracting sub-spans of cross-lingual title pairs and aligning with GIZA++; (7) translate mentions and run unsupervised collective linking by comparing constructed context knowledge networks to candidate entity networks using salience/similarity/coherence metrics. Empirically, models trained on the silver data reach high F-scores (>~80%) and linking accuracies (>~80%) on Wikipedia-derived test splits for many languages (especially where mentions >30K), and on nine external Non-Wikipedia languages the silver-trained models are within ~5.8–17.6% absolute F-score of gold-supervised models; morphology and self-training ablations show measurable gains (e.g., Turkish/Uzbeks morphology gains, Turkish self-training gains). The paper claims large-scale resource release (annotations, analyzers, systems) and positions the contribution as an integrated engineering/resource advance rather than new core learning algorithms. Uncertainties remain about propagation noise, AMR-to-YAGO mapping reliability, translation coverage/quality, end-to-end linking recall (NIL/unlinkable mentions), and the degree to which silver-derived high scores generalize to true human gold performance.

concerns.description: Propagation of English-page labels to 282 languages hinges on interlanguage/redirect links being present and correct; in many low-resource languages these links are missing or noisy leading to sparse or incorrect propagated labels.

Shared analysis notes coverage is limited and alignments from short title pairs can be noisy.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report statistics: fraction of mentions with any mined translation, precision/recall of translations on a sampled set, and ablation showing linking performance when using only high-confidence pairs vs. all pairs; consider alternative alignment tools or subword-aware methods.

concerns.title: Morphology extraction limited to concatenative affixation

Gains reported only for Turkish and Uzbek (Section 4.2).

counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If interlanguage links are largely correct and present for the entities of interest, propagation will yield high-quality multilingual labels.
If DBpedia/YAGO properties are sufficiently populated and discriminative for many English pages, English classification will be accurate and reduce propagation noise.
If mined title-pair translations achieve adequate precision and coverage for a language, unsupervised linking to an English KB will succeed for a useful fraction of mentions.
If self-training seeds are high-precision and clustering effectively groups clean contexts, bootstrapping will expand coverage without amplifying noise.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues that a fully automatic, KB-mined pipeline can produce "silver-standard" multilingual name annotations and train taggers and linkers for 282 Wikipedia languages without any human annotation or native-speaker input. The pipeline reasoning chain is: (1) map a small English AMR-annotated set to YAGO types via PMI to obtain multi-granularity typing schemas; (2) train type classifiers on English Wikipedia pages using DBpedia/YAGO properties as language-agnostic features; (3) propagate those page-level types to mentions in other-language Wikipedia pages via cross-lingual and redirect links to create initial silver labels; (4) expand and clean annotations via self-training seeded by NPMI-selected high-confidence sentences and clusterwise iterative labeling; (5) derive morphology cues (affix/stem heuristics) from Wikipedia anchor markups to improve tagging for morphologically rich languages; (6) mine word/phrase translation pairs from exhaustive sub-span extraction of cross-lingual Wikipedia title pairs and align with GIZA++ to enable translation of mentions to English; (7) perform unsupervised collective linking by building knowledge networks (KNs) for translated mentions and KB candidates, scoring by salience/similarity/coherence; (8) evaluate at scale on Wikipedia-derived silver test splits (70/30) and on nine external Non-Wikipedia datasets (LORELEI) to compare against gold-trained supervised systems and language-independent baselines. Empirical results show high within-silver-domain predictability (many languages >80% F when mention counts are large) and a non-Wikipedia gap of ~5.8–17.6% absolute F relative to supervised gold-trained models. The manuscript emphasizes engineering scale, several novel KB-mining ideas (AMR→YAGO mapping; DBpedia property features; morphology from anchor markups; exhaustive title-span translation mining) and provides resource releases for 282 languages.
logical_argument_graph: L1: Need: provide entity-level information across many languages without per-language annotation.
L2: Leverage Wikipedia and structured KBs (DBpedia/YAGO) which already link pages across languages and contain properties.
L3: Use AMR-annotated English mentions to map fine-grained AMR types to YAGO via PMI to obtain a multi-granular typing schema.
L4: Train English-page classifiers using DBpedia/YAGO properties as features so classification is independent of target-language NLP tools.
L5: Propagate English-page labels to other-language mentions via cross-lingual/redirect links to create silver-standard mention annotations across 282 languages.
L6: Improve coverage/quality by self-training on unlabeled sentences using NPMI-seeded high-confidence examples and clusterwise iterative addition.
L7: Customize training selection (commonness and topical relatedness) for rapid domain adaptation in emergent scenarios.
L8: Extract morphology signals (stems/affixes) from anchor-markup pairs for morphologically-rich languages and include these as features in tagging models.
L9: Mine translation pairs from cross-lingual title sub-spans with GIZA++ to enable translating mentions to English beyond exact title matches.

L10: For linking, translate mentions, generate candidate entities from a surface-form dictionary, construct knowledge networks for both mentions and candidates, and score candidate matches by salience/similarity/coherence to pick links.
L11: Evaluate: within-Wikipedia silver splits measure predictability; external Non-Wikipedia (9 languages) compare to gold-supervised systems to estimate real-world generalization.
L12: Conclude the approach yields useful silver annotations and competitive non-gold performance, and that releasing resources for 282 languages offers a valuable benchmark.
