concerns.title: AMR→YAGO mapping trained on a very small AMR sample
concerns.description: PMI-based mapping from AMR types to YAGO uses only 2,756 AMR mentions, making fine-grained type alignment potentially noisy and brittle across the large YAGO hierarchy.
evidence: Section 2.2: AMR corpus contains 2,756 mentions used to compute PMI to 9,154 YAGO types.
Shared analysis notes small AMR sample may introduce noise.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide: (a) quantitative diagnostics of AMR→YAGO mapping quality (confusion matrix, top-k mapping precision), (b) manual spot-checks of sample mappings for several fine-grained YAGO types, and (c) ablation showing downstream impact when using coarser mappings only.

concerns.title: Dependence on interlanguage/redirect link correctness and coverage
concerns.description: The projection step assumes Wikipedia cross-lingual links reliably connect equivalent entities across languages; missing/incorrect links will propagate wrong or incomplete labels, especially in low-resource languages.
evidence: Section 2.2: propagate English page labels to mentions via cross-lingual links.
Assumption A1 in shared analysis emphasizes the risk if interlanguage links are missing or incorrect.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide statistics on interlanguage link coverage and error rates across a representative sample of low-, mid-, and high-resource languages; include fallback strategies (e.g., TITLE translation heuristics) when links are missing.

concerns.title: Translation mining coverage and noise not fully quantified
concerns.description: Mining word translations from short title pairs and extracting alignments with GIZA++ can be noisy; manuscript shows examples but lacks systematic coverage/precision metrics tying mined translations to linking performance.
evidence: Section 3.2 describes exhaustive sub-span extraction and shows Table 2 examples, but lacks coverage and precision breakdown.
Shared analysis notes only a small percentage of mentions are exact title matches.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report (a) proportion of mentions that obtain at least one translation candidate from the mined dictionary per language, (b) precision of top-k mined translation pairs via manual spot-checks in several languages, and (c) sensitivity of linking accuracy to translation dictionary pruning thresholds.

concerns.title: Self-training risks of error amplification and limited cross-language validation
concerns.description: The self-training loop seeded by NPMI and clusterwise expansion may amplify early errors; empirical improvement is shown mainly for Turkish, leaving cross-language robustness uncertain.
evidence: Section 2.3 details NPMI seed selection (τ=0) and n=20 clusters; Section 4.3 reports Turkish gains only.
Shared analysis flags risk that self-training can amplify noisy seeds.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include ablation experiments disabling self-training across multiple typologically diverse languages and add label-noise simulations (injecting controlled noise into seeds) to measure robustness.

concerns.title: Morphology-from-anchors limited to concatenative morphologies
concerns.description: Affix extraction from anchor-markups only works when stems and affixes are concatenated and anchor markup coverage is sufficient; non-concatenative morphologies, clitics, or languages without tokenization remain unaddressed.
evidence: Section 2.5 explicitly notes approach limited to concatenative affixation and tokenization; experiments reported for Turkish and Uzbek only.
Shared analysis highlights non-applicability to non-concatenative languages.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify scope: enumerate language families where the method applies, and quantify anchor-derived affix coverage. Consider integrating unsupervised morphology learners (Morfessor) as a complement for other languages.

concerns.title: Linking evaluation ignores unlinkable and NIL cases
concerns.description: Linking accuracy is reported only for mentions with surface-form candidate matches; excluding unlinkable mentions masks end-to-end recall and overall utility of the system.
evidence: Section 4.1: 'we only compute linking accuracy for linkable name mentions' and candidate generation relies on surface-form dictionary.
Shared analysis notes exclusion hides recall failures.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report end-to-end linking metrics: precision/recall/F1 including recall over all mentions (linkable and unlinkable), provide NIL detection rates, and show candidate generation coverage per language.

comparable_works.relevance: Prior work constructing NER labels from Wikipedia and manually curating English pages; used as a baseline comparison.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar in leveraging Wikipedia anchors; differs by being manual/semi-manual labeling and covering far fewer languages and coarser types. This manuscript automates typing via KB properties and AMR mappings and scales to 282 languages.
comparable_works.source_trace: Manuscript references; Nothman et al. cited in Sections 1,2,5

comparable_works.relevance: Unsupervised entity linking with AMR and knowledge-network similarity measures used as a methodological precedent for KN construction and scoring.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Manuscript reuses salience/similarity/coherence scoring described by Pan et al., but extends cross-lingual mention translation and large-scale surface-form mining.
comparable_works.source_trace: Manuscript Section 3.3; referenced in linking description

comparable_works.citation_label: Zhang et al. 2016a; Zhang et al. 2016b
comparable_works.relevance: LORELEI-era work on low-resource NER and bitext projection; used as comparison baselines on Non-Wikipedia data.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Zhang et al. rely on English annotations and projection or expectation-driven learning; manuscript claims competitive performance without such annotated inputs.

comparable_works.relevance: Cross-lingual NER via wikification; used as a baseline for language-independent methods.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Tsai et al. use projection from English wikified data; the present work tries to avoid English-to-target projection reliance by using DBpedia properties and fully automatic propagation.

comparable_works.relevance: Work aiming to extend cross-lingual entity linking to many Wikipedia languages using supervised linkers.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Sil & Florian use supervised methods trained with Wikipedia links; the present work differs by pursuing unsupervised collective linking aided by mined translations for many more languages.

comparable_works.relevance: Reference for NPMI-based seed selection used in self-training.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Manuscript adopts Guo et al.'s idea for seed selection but scales it within its clusterwise iterative self-training across many languages.

comparable_works.relevance: Provides the multilingual YAGO KB used for type hierarchies and properties.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Manuscript leverages YAGO/DBpedia properties as features; YAGO3 is the source KB helpful for multilingual mappings.

uncertainty_flags: High reliance on silver-standard test splits that are generated by the same pipeline as training confounds true generalization estimates.
AMR→YAGO mapping is estimated from a small AMR sample (2,756 mentions) making fine-grained typing mappings uncertain.
Coverage and correctness of interlanguage links vary by language and are critical to propagation quality.
Mined translation dictionaries lack reported coverage/precision metrics across languages; their effect on end-to-end linking is uncertain.
Self-training improvements are demonstrated mainly for Turkish; cross-lingual robustness and failure modes are underexplored.
Linking metrics exclude unlinkable mentions; end-to-end recall and NIL handling are unclear.
alternative_interpretations: High in-domain (Wikipedia) scores may reflect the system’s ability to reproduce the pipeline's heuristics rather than accurate human-quality extraction; the system fits its own noise.
DBpedia/YAGO properties may be acting as proxies for canonical page-type signals rather than creating a genuinely language-agnostic typing feature set; strong English-side signal could be dominating.

The apparent competitiveness on Non-Wikipedia data for nine languages could be influenced by the selected languages being relatively well-covered or similar to English in entity coverage; other low-resource languages may show larger gaps.
Morphology gains seen for Turkish/Uzbek may be due mainly to high anchor coverage for specific affix patterns in Wikipedia rather than a general morphological analysis capability.
transparency_notes: Key hyperparameters are reported (e.g., NPMI τ=0, clustering n=20, training selection D=30,000) but sensitivity analyses are limited.

Metrics for critical intermediate artifacts (AMR→YAGO mapping quality, translation-pair precision/recall, interlanguage-link coverage, candidate-generation coverage) are not fully presented and should be included for reproducibility.
Evaluation on external gold data is limited to nine languages; broader human-evaluated sampling across language families is required to substantiate general claims about 282 languages.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The manuscript introduces several ideas that lack direct one-to-one precedents (AMR→YAGO mapping to create multi-granular types; extracting affixes from anchor markups at scale; exhaustive title-subspan translation mining). Sparse precedent should be treated as an innovation signal, but these ideas still require targeted empirical validation—novelty alone does not imply correctness.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: High interlanguage link coverage and correctness across target languages (so English page labels reliably map to target-language mentions).
Sufficient DBpedia/YAGO property density and consistency per entity to make property-based classifiers discriminative.
AMR→YAGO mapping quality improves with additional annotated data or tighter mapping heuristics so that fine-grained types are accurate.
Mined translation dictionaries have adequate coverage and precision for candidate generation, or complementary transliteration/fallback methods are available.
Self-training seed selection is robust across typological varieties and does not systematically propagate early mistakes.

novelty_lenses.verdict: supports novelty as a meaningful conceptual frame
novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper assembles multiple KB-mining operations into a single fully automatic cross-lingual pipeline at an unprecedented scale (282 languages); several individual components (anchor-derived morphology, AMR→YAGO multi-granular typing, exhaustive title-subspan translation mining) are not standard in the literature and represent potentially disruptive approaches to zero-human multilingual IE.
evidence: Sections 2.2, 2.5, 3.2 describe new operationalizations (AMR→YAGO mapping, affix extraction, title-subspan mining) with examples and localized performance improvements.
Resource release for 282 languages is much larger in scope than most prior Wikipedia-based NER/linking efforts cited (Nothman et al., McNamee et al., Sil & Florian).
uncertainty_flags: Novelty is evident but its validity depends on robustness diagnostics (AMR mapping quality, translation coverage, interlanguage link reliability), which are currently underreported.

novelty_lenses.verdict: partly incremental with important engineering scaling
novelty_lenses.rationale: While individual ideas borrow from prior distant supervision and projection literature, the main contribution can be seen as an engineering and integration advance that scales those ideas massively; thus the work is partly incremental in method but novel in breadth and combination.
evidence: Manuscript cites and builds on prior approaches such as Nothman et al. (Wikipedia anchors), Pan et al. (KN-based linking), Guo et al. (NPMI seeds), and Zhang/Tsai (LORELEI baselines).
The use of DBpedia properties for classifier features is a pragmatic extension of KB-driven distant supervision.
uncertainty_flags: Degree of methodological novelty vs. engineering scaling is ambiguous until deeper component-level validation is shown.

novelty_lenses.verdict: concerns about evaluation and artifact measurement temper novelty claims
novelty_lenses.rationale: The approach is creative, but the heavy reliance on silver test splits and omission of end-to-end recall/NIL metrics weaken demonstration of practical validity; novelty must be paired with rigorous diagnostics to be persuasive.
evidence: Section 4.1's 70/30 silver split evaluation and Section 4.2's nine-language external evaluation are useful but insufficient to validate claims across 282 languages.
Assumptions A1, A2, A3 in shared analysis highlight risks that directly affect validity.
uncertainty_flags: Greater empirical transparency (human spot checks, coverage statistics) could increase confidence in methodological soundness.

confidence_interval.rationale: I have moderate-to-high confidence in the descriptive reconstruction of the paper's methods and in the identified strengths/concerns because the manuscript provides many concrete implementation details and experimental tables. However, uncertainty remains about the robustness and generalizability of key novel components (AMR→YAGO mapping, mined translations, interlanguage link reliability) due to missing diagnostics, hence a non-extreme confidence interval.

prior_stage_inputs: Shared analysis of extracted claims, assumptions, argument focus, evaluation targets, and prior-stage digests from four reviewers (structure_analyst, methodology_auditor, novelty_assessor_incremental, novelty_assessor_disruptive).
Manuscript excerpts and tables (Sections 1-6, Tables 1-5, Table 3 large per-language table, experiments on Wikipedia 70/30 split and nine LORELEI languages).
Retrieved background literature and ARR reviewer guideline context.
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: Reconstructing the manuscript's reasoning: The authors build an end-to-end, fully automatic pipeline that (1) induces multi-granular entity types by mapping AMR fine-grained types to the YAGO hierarchy using PMI computed on an AMR corpus, (2) trains English-page classifiers using DBpedia/YAGO entity properties (language-independent features) and propagates page-level types to mentions in 282 languages via interlanguage/redirect links and anchor markups to form silver-standard annotations, (3) expands and cleans annotations with NPMI-seeded iterative self-training and clusterwise labeling, (4) selects topical/common training sentences for rapid adaptation, (5) derives morphology (affix/stem) features from bracketed anchor markups, (6) mines word/phrase translation pairs from exhaustive sub-span extraction of cross-lingual title pairs aligned with GIZA++, and (7) uses an unsupervised collective linking method comparing knowledge networks (salience/similarity/coherence) to link translated mentions to English DBpedia. Empirically, the pipeline attains high tagging F-scores and linking accuracy on Wikipedia-derived silver test splits for many languages (performance strongly correlated with mention counts), shows morphology and self-training gains on select languages (Turkish/Uzbek), and achieves silver-trained models within ~5.8–17.6% absolute F of gold-trained models on nine non-Wikipedia LORELEI languages. Evidence supports the pipeline's internal consistency and scalability; however, key claims are partially supported because core evaluations largely use silver-standard splits generated by the same pipeline, some modules (AMR→YAGO mapping, translation mining) rely on small or sparse data, and end-to-end linking recall (including unlinkable/NIL cases) is not fully reported. I flag uncertainty where claims extrapolate broader generalization from limited out-of-domain evaluation and where assumptions about interlanguage link and KB property quality are central to success.
logical_argument_graph: A1: AMR mentions (2,756) + PMI -> map AMR types to YAGO types (multi-granularity typing).
A2: DBpedia/YAGO entity properties used as language-independent features -> train English page classifiers for types.
A3: Propagate English page types via interlanguage/redirect links and anchor markups -> silver-standard mention annotations across 282 languages.
A4: Initial silver labels are incomplete/noisy -> apply NPMI-seeded self-training + clusterwise iterative labeling to expand/clean annotations.
A5: For rapid/adaptive training, select sentences by entity commonness and topical relatedness (English Leidos/LORELEI pipeline).
A6: Extract affix/stem features from bracketed anchor markups -> morphology features improve tagging for morphologically rich languages.
A7: Exhaustive sub-span extraction of cross-lingual title pairs + GIZA++ -> mined word/phrase translation pairs for name translation.
A8: Translate mentions and run unsupervised collective linking (KN similarity: salience/similarity/coherence) -> link translated mentions to English DBpedia.
E1: Evaluate on Wikipedia 70/30 silver splits -> high F-scores and linking accuracy correlated with mention counts.
E2: Evaluate on nine Non-Wikipedia LORELEI languages -> silver-trained models within ~5.8–17.6% of gold models and outperform some baselines.

Conclusion: Fully automatic KB-mined pipeline produces useful silver-standard annotations and viable taggers/linkers for 282 languages without manual/native input, with caveats about coverage, label noise, and end-to-end recall.

identified_claims.claim_text: A fully automatic pipeline that mines Wikipedia markups and KB properties (DBpedia/YAGO) can produce useful silver-standard name annotations and train name taggers for 282 languages without manual labels or native-speaker input.
evidence: Section 2.2: describes English-page typing using AMR and DBpedia properties and propagation via cross-lingual links.
Section 4.1 and Table 3: report name tagging F-scores per language from silver 70/30 splits across 282 languages.
Conclusions: authors state release of silver-standard annotations and systems for 282 languages.
uncertainty_flags: The term 'useful' is underspecified; 'useful' is supported in-domain (silver test) but external gold-standard evidence limited to nine languages.
Evaluation on silver test splits can inflate scores because train and test share the same annotation heuristics and noise.
Coverage and quality vary widely across languages (performance correlates strongly with mention count).

identified_claims.claim_text: Leveraging AMR annotations and mappings to the YAGO type hierarchy together with DBpedia/YAGO properties yields multi-granularity entity typing that generalizes across languages.
evidence: Section 2.2: authors compute PMI between AMR types and YAGO types to produce 4 coarse types, 139 AMR types, and 9,154 YAGO types.
Section 2.2: Maximum Entropy classifiers trained with DBpedia properties produce labels for 10M English pages.
uncertainty_flags: AMR→YAGO mapping is computed from a small AMR corpus (2,756 mentions), raising concerns about noise and the reliability of fine-grained mappings.
Generalization across languages depends on correct cross-lingual links; mapping quality beyond English is not directly validated against human-annotated gold types.

identified_claims.claim_text: Using entity properties from DBpedia as features eliminates the need for language-specific features/resources (e.g., POS tags) when classifying English KB pages and propagating types cross-lingually.
evidence: Section 2.2: description of using properties like birthDate, population as features and training Maximum Entropy classifiers.
Table 1: features include KB-derived gazetteer, embeddings and entity properties.
uncertainty_flags: DBpedia/YAGO coverage and cleanliness are heterogeneous; sparse/noisy properties will produce misclassifications that propagate across languages.
This reduces reliance on language-specific features for English-side classification but assumes propagated labels remain valid in target languages.

identified_claims.claim_text: Self-training (iterative bootstrapping with NPMI-based seed selection and cluster-wise addition of high-confidence predictions) substantially refines and increases coverage of automatically generated annotations.
evidence: Section 2.3: details NPMI(seed) selection (τ=0) and clustering (n=20) with iterative labeling.
Section 4.3: Turkish learning curve shows 6% absolute gain on Wikipedia and 12% on Non-Wikipedia after self-training.
uncertainty_flags: Empirical self-training improvements are demonstrated mainly for Turkish; cross-language generality is not comprehensively quantified.
Self-training risks amplification of label noise if seeds/confidence estimates are unreliable, especially in low-resource languages.

identified_claims.claim_label: training data selection via commonness and topicality
identified_claims.claim_text: Cross-lingual topic transfer and ranking by entity commonness and topical relatedness allow selection of high-quality annotated sentences for training, useful for rapid adaptation in scenarios like disasters.
evidence: Section 2.4: dynamic frequency thresholding for commonness and topical relatedness using English tagger+linker on the Leidos/LORELEI corpus to select top Wikipedia categories.
uncertainty_flags: No quantitative ablation provided showing the numerical benefit of this selection across the broad language set.
Topical selection depends on English resources and assumes topics transfer cleanly across languages and cultures.

identified_claims.claim_label: morphology from Wiki markups improves performance
identified_claims.claim_text: Deriving affix lists and stemming heuristics from Wikipedia markups provides morphology features that improve name tagging for morphologically rich languages (e.g., Turkish, Uzbek).
evidence: Section 2.5: method for extracting suffixes from bracketed anchor forms (Turkish example) and using them as features.
Section 4.2: reported absolute F-score gains of 11.1% for Turkish and 7.1% for Uzbek from morphology features.
uncertainty_flags: Method only applies to concatenative morphology where stem+affix are contiguous; languages with non-concatenative morphology or languages lacking anchors will not benefit.
Reported gains are demonstrated for two languages; broader cross-lingual generality is not shown.

identified_claims.claim_label: mining word translations from title pairs
identified_claims.claim_text: Mining word translation pairs from cross-lingual Wikipedia title pairs via exhaustive sub-span extraction and GIZA++ alignment produces useful translation pairs that enable name translation and linking.
evidence: Section 3.2: exhaustive generation of continuous token combinations from titles and running GIZA++ to extract word translations.
Table 2: examples of mined word translation pairs with alignment confidences.
uncertainty_flags: Coverage is limited; only a small percentage of mentions are exact title matches, and aggregate coverage/precision statistics are not provided.
Alignments from short title pairs can be noisy; the impact of noisy translations on linking is not quantified.

identified_claims.claim_text: An unsupervised collective inference approach that constructs knowledge networks from context and compares salience/similarity/coherence with KB candidate networks can link translated mentions to English DBpedia with high accuracy for linkable mentions.
evidence: Section 3.3: description of constructing KNs for translated mentions and candidate KB entities and scoring similarity per Pan et al. (2015).
Section 4.1 / Table 3: linking accuracy often >80% for many languages on Wikipedia-derived linkable mentions.
uncertainty_flags: Linking accuracy is reported only on mentions deemed linkable (surface-form coverage); unlinkable/NIL recall and end-to-end coverage are not reported.
Candidate generation via surface-form dictionary may miss entities or produce noisy candidates; recall impact is unclear.

identified_claims.claim_text: On Wikipedia-derived test data the framework attains high tagging F-scores (> ~80%) and linking accuracy (> ~80%) for many languages; performance strongly correlates with number of mentions per language (e.g., >30K mentions usually >80% F-score).
evidence: Section 4.1: authors report F-scores generally >80% when mention counts >30K and big drops when mentions <250.
Table 3: large per-language table showing mention counts, F-scores, and linking accuracies across 282 languages.
uncertainty_flags: Evaluation uses silver-standard 70/30 splits; high predictability within silver data does not necessarily imply human-level accuracy on gold annotations.
Large per-language variance suggests thresholds where system becomes unreliable; explicit per-language KB/anchor coverage statistics are missing.

identified_claims.claim_text: On external news/forum datasets in nine languages, models trained on silver-standard annotations achieve performance that approaches supervised gold-trained models, with absolute F-score gaps of ~5.8–17.6%, and outperform some prior language-independent baselines.
evidence: Section 4.2: comparisons to gold-trained supervised models and language-independent baselines (Zhang et al., 2016a; Tsai et al., 2016) showing silver models are 5.8–17.6% lower F.
Tables 4 and 5: Non-Wikipedia dataset sizes and per-language F-scores.
uncertainty_flags: Out-of-domain evaluation is limited to nine LORELEI languages; selection may bias representativeness across scripts and typologies.
Some baseline entries are missing; direct apples-to-apples comparability and statistical significance tests are not presented.

strengths.title: Impressive language-scale engineering
strengths.description: The pipeline is applied end-to-end to 282 Wikipedia languages and includes tagging, fine/coarse-grained typing, morphology analyzers, and linking components.
evidence: Paper claims resource generation and system release for 282 languages (Abstract, Conclusions).
Table 3 provides per-language statistics across hundreds of languages.

strengths.title: Creative use of KB-derived, language-independent features
strengths.description: Using DBpedia/YAGO entity properties to classify English pages avoids language-specific preprocessing and supports cross-lingual propagation.
evidence: Section 2.2: training Maximum Entropy models with DBpedia properties (birthDate, population) as features; Table 1 features.
Compared favourably to Nothman et al. (2012) classification (96.0% F vs 94.6%) on a cited dataset.

strengths.title: Multiple practical modules integrated
strengths.description: Pipeline integrates AMR→YAGO typing, self-training, topical selection, morphology extraction from anchors, translation mining, and unsupervised linking into a cohesive system.
evidence: Section-level description enumerates each module (Sections 2.2–3.3).
Empirical ablations: morphology gains (Turkish/Uzbek) and self-training gains (Turkish).

strengths.title: Demonstrated morphology benefit on morphologically rich languages
strengths.description: Affix mining from anchor markups yields substantial absolute F-score improvements for Turkish and Uzbek.
evidence: Section 4.2: morphology features contributed 11.1% and 7.1% absolute F gains for Turkish and Uzbek, respectively.
Section 2.5: explanation and Turkish example of affix extraction.

concerns.title: Reliance on silver-standard within-domain evaluation
concerns.description: Major performance claims are supported mainly by 70/30 splits of silver-standard data produced by the same pipeline; this risks circular validation and may overestimate real-world accuracy against human gold annotations.
evidence: Section 4.1: 70% training / 30% testing on selected Wikipedia sentences from pipeline annotations.
Shared analysis and prior reviewers note possible overestimation due to shared heuristics/noise.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide human-annotated sample evaluations (span, type, link) across diverse language families (incl. low-mention and non-Latin scripts) and report precision/recall vs. gold annotations; or perform cross-pipeline holdout where annotations are produced by an independently configured pipeline variant.

concerns.title: Small AMR sample for AMR→YAGO mapping
concerns.description: The AMR-to-YAGO mapping is estimated using only 2,756 AMR mentions, which is small relative to the 9,154 YAGO types, risking noisy fine-grained type mappings that may mislead classifiers.
evidence: Section 2.2: AMR corpus has 2,756 mentions; mapping uses PMI to YAGO types.
Prior-stage digest highlights mapping noise and limited signal for fine-grained typing.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report mapping quality metrics (precision@k of mapped types), provide examples of high/low-confidence mappings, and consider thresholding to restrict fine-grained types to those with robust PMI support or augment mapping with additional distant supervision.

concerns.title: Unclear end-to-end linking recall and NIL handling
concerns.description: Linking accuracy is reported only for 'linkable' mentions (those with surface-form candidates), omitting unlinkable mentions and NIL prediction recall; end-to-end utility and coverage remain unclear.
evidence: Section 3.3 and 4.1: authors state they only compute linking accuracy for linkable mentions; no recall/NIL statistics provided.
Shared analysis: omission hides candidate generation coverage and end-to-end performance.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report candidate-generation coverage (fraction of mentions with at least one candidate), end-to-end linking precision/recall/F including NIL decisions, and qualitative examples of common NIL/false-link cases.

concerns.title: Translation mining coverage and noise not quantified
concerns.description: The word/phrase translation extraction via exhaustive title sub-spans and GIZA++ is promising, but the manuscript lacks aggregate metrics for coverage, precision, and error impact on linking across languages.
evidence: Section 3.2 and Table 2 show examples but no global coverage/precision numbers.
Shared analysis notes only small percentage of mentions are exact title matches and alignments on short titles can be noisy.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide statistics: number of translation pairs per language, precision estimates (human spot-check or automatic proxy), coverage of mention types, and ablation showing linking accuracy with/without mined translations.

concerns.title: Self-training robustness not validated across typologies
concerns.description: Self-training gains are shown for Turkish but broader cross-language robustness (especially in low-mention or nonspace scripts) is not demonstrated; self-training may amplify errors where seed signals are weak.
evidence: Section 4.3: only Turkish learning curves reported (6% Wikipedia, 12% Non-Wikipedia gains).
Shared analysis warns self-training can amplify noise where NPMI seeds/clustering fail.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide multi-language self-training ablations (representative sample across high/medium/low mention counts and script types) and error analysis showing whether errors are amplified or corrected during iterations.

concerns.title: Dependency on interlanguage link quality and KB property coverage
concerns.description: Propagation of English types depends on accurate interlanguage links and sufficiently rich DBpedia/YAGO properties; missing or incorrect links/properties will cause label sparsity and noise in many low-resource languages.
evidence: Section 2.2: propagation via cross-lingual and redirect links; Section 2.2 and assumptions A1/A2 in shared analysis.
Shared reviewers repeatedly flagged variable interlanguage link coverage.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report per-language statistics: fraction of pages with interlanguage links, average number of properties per entity, and correlation analyses between these KB coverage metrics and tagging/linking performance; discuss mitigation strategies for low-coverage languages.

concerns.title: Limited out-of-domain evaluation
concerns.description: Non-Wikipedia evaluation is limited to nine LORELEI languages (news/forum), which is useful but insufficient to claim broad generalization to diverse non-Wikipedia domains and scripts.
evidence: Section 4.2: non-Wikipedia experiments cover nine languages; reported gaps vs. gold-trained models are 5.8–17.6% absolute F.
Shared analysis highlights the limited representativeness of these nine languages.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Extend out-of-domain tests to more languages and domains (social media, local news) emphasizing typological diversity (space-less scripts, non-Latin, morphologically complex) or, if unfeasible, provide targeted sampled human evaluations on additional languages to support generalization claims.

comparable_works.relevance: Prior work using Wikipedia to create multilingual NER training data; manual mapping/classification of English pages.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar in leveraging Wikipedia anchors; differs because current paper uses KB properties and AMR→YAGO to automate typing and scales to 282 languages without manual labels.

comparable_works.relevance: Unsupervised linking using Abstract Meaning Representation and knowledge-network similarity; used as methodological baseline for linking scoring (salience/similarity/coherence).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: The manuscript adapts their KN-similarity measures in a cross-lingual setting after translation; similarity in collective inference approach.

comparable_works.citation_label: Zhang et al. 2016a; Tsai et al. 2016
comparable_works.relevance: Recent LORELEI-era methods for low-resource name tagging used as baselines in Non-Wikipedia experiments.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Those approaches often require English projection or native-speaker input; the current work claims no manual input and shows competitive performance on nine languages.

comparable_works.relevance: Source for YAGO knowledge base and multilingual coverage; relevant for KB-derived features and type hierarchy.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Manuscript builds on YAGO/DBpedia structures whereas YAGO3 is the KB resource; difference is in mapping AMR types to YAGO and mining properties for classification.

comparable_works.relevance: Standard word alignment toolkit used to mine translation pairs from title pairs.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Method is standard; innovation is exhaustive sub-span extraction applied to title pairs for short-text alignments.

uncertainty_flags: Primary large-scale metrics are computed on silver-standard test data produced by the same pipeline; this creates validation circularity and may overestimate absolute quality.
AMR→YAGO fine-grained mappings derived from only 2,756 AMR mentions risk noisy mappings for many YAGO types.
Interlanguage link and DBpedia property coverage vary greatly by language; performance likely degrades where these signals are sparse.
Linking evaluation excludes unlinkable mentions and NIL handling; end-to-end recall and system utility are not fully reported.
Translation mining coverage and precision across languages are not quantified; noisy translations can harm linking.
alternative_interpretations: High F-scores on Wikipedia 70/30 splits may reflect label consistency with the annotation heuristics (anchors and propagated page types) rather than semantic correctness compared to human gold labels.

Morphology and self-training gains shown for select languages (Turkish/Uzbek) may be due to particularly favorable anchor/KB coverage in those Wikipedias and may not generalize to other morphologically rich but low-coverage languages.

The reported closeness to gold-trained models on nine languages could be driven by domain similarity between English resources used for topical selection and the evaluated datasets, not by intrinsic cross-lingual robustness.
transparency_notes: The manuscript provides detailed module descriptions and empirical tables, but lacks certain reproducibility metrics: per-language KB property coverage, candidate-generation coverage, NIL/unlinkable rates, and mapping quality scores for AMR→YAGO.

The paper claims to release datasets/systems for 282 languages; reviewers should verify the availability of code, extraction scripts, and raw silver annotations to enable replication and independent audits.

Important hyperparameters (e.g., thresholds for translation alignment confidences, GIZA++ configurations, NPMI τ, clustering details) should be fully enumerated in supplementary materials for reproducibility.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The pipeline assembles several known components (AMR/YAGO, DBpedia properties, self-training, GIZA++ alignment, KN linking) but their integration at unprecedented language scale (282 languages) and the morphology-from-anchor idea are relatively novel; lack of close analogs is an innovation signal but does not by itself validate empirical claims—robust evaluation is still required.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If interlanguage links and DBpedia properties are plentiful and accurate for a target language, propagation will produce high-quality silver labels and the pipeline will work well.

If AMR→YAGO mappings are filtered to high-PMI, and translation pairs are validated or thresholded, self-training is seeded with high-precision instances, and candidate generation covers most surface forms, then the linking component can achieve high end-to-end accuracy.

If released resources include confidence scores for propagated labels and mined translations, downstream users can safely threshold to trade coverage for precision, making the resource practically useful even if noisy.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Applying a cohesive KB-mining and cross-lingual pipeline to 282 languages with release of silver annotations and models is a substantial engineering/resource contribution, with value to researchers and applications.
evidence: Claims and Table 3 covering hundreds of languages; Section 6 release promise.
uncertainty_flags: Value depends on released data quality and documentation (confidence scores, per-language coverage).

novelty_lenses.rationale: Individual components (AMR→YAGO mapping via PMI, DBpedia property feature use, affix extraction from anchors, exhaustive title sub-span alignment) are incremental combinations of existing ideas but adapted in useful ways; the affix-from-anchor technique is a targeted, low-cost morphology heuristic with demonstrated gains.
evidence: Section 2.5 morphology gains; Section 3.2 translation mining scheme; mapping described in Section 2.2.
uncertainty_flags: Mapping robustness and generality beyond examples need stronger validation.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Within-silver-domain predictability is strongly evidenced (large per-language table), and select out-of-domain tests show promising but variable gaps versus supervised models; however, the heavy reliance on silver test data weakens claims about real-world absolute accuracy.
evidence: Section 4.1 Wikipedia 70/30 results and Section 4.2 Non-Wikipedia LORELEI comparisons (nine languages).
uncertainty_flags: Need human gold comparisons across typologically diverse languages and end-to-end recall reporting.

confidence_interval.rationale: My calibrated confidence (expressed as probability that the main claim—'fully automatic KB-mined pipeline produces broadly useful and generalizable taggers/linkers for 282 languages without manual input'—is substantially supported as stated) is moderate-to-low. Evidence strongly supports within-silver-domain predictability and engineering scale, but key generalization claims (across typologies, end-to-end linking coverage, fine-grained typing reliability) are uncertain due to dependence on small AMR sample, silver-only evaluation for most languages, and missing metrics (NIL recall, KB coverage). The interval reflects substantial evidence for engineering results but notable methodological/evaluation gaps that could materially affect claim strength.

consensus_findings: The manuscript describes a coherent, fully automatic end-to-end pipeline that mines Wikipedia markups and KB properties (DBpedia/YAGO) to produce silver-standard span/type/link annotations and train tagger/linker systems across a very large set of languages (claimed 282).

Engineering/scale contribution is substantial: integrating typing (AMR->YAGO), DBpedia/YAGO-based English classification, cross-lingual propagation, self-training, anchor-derived morphology, title-subspan translation mining, and unsupervised collective linking at this breadth is novel as an engineering/resource effort.

Within-Wikipedia (silver-derived) evaluations report high in-domain predictability (many languages with >~80% F-score and linking accuracy when mention counts are large), and selected ablations (morphology, self-training) show measurable gains in the languages reported (e.g., Turkish, Uzbek).

Out-of-domain (Non-Wikipedia) tests on nine LORELEI languages show silver-trained models approach supervised gold-trained models in some cases (reported gaps ~5.8–17.6% absolute F), indicating potential practical utility for some languages/domains.

Key methodological dependencies are repeatedly identified and agreed upon: reliance on interlanguage links for propagation, on DBpedia/YAGO property coverage and quality for typing, on a small AMR sample for fine-grained mapping, and on title-pair alignments for mined translations and linking candidate coverage.
disagreements: Interpretation of the empirical strength: some reviewers emphasize that within-silver high scores meaningfully demonstrate pipeline predictability and engineering success, while others caution that those same scores may largely reflect consistency with the pipeline's own labeling heuristics (circular validation) and therefore overestimate human-gold performance.

Novelty framing: reviewers differ on whether the paper's contribution is primarily a large-scale incremental integration of known methods (most reviewers) or whether particular components (AMR->YAGO multi-granularity typing, anchor-derived morphology, exhaustive title-subspan mining) should be read as more disruptive innovations; all agree the scale magnifies impact.

Extent of concern severity: reviewers uniformly flag evaluation gaps (silver-test dependence, lack of end-to-end linking recall/NIL rates, small AMR sample), but they vary in how much these gaps undercut the paper's principal claims — some call them major methodological flaws needing remediation, others rate them as addressable with additional diagnostics and selective human evaluation.
uncertainty_hotspots: Silver-vs-gold validity: primary large-scale results are reported on silver-standard test splits produced by the same automated pipeline, creating risk that reported high scores reflect label/heuristic consistency rather than human-level correctness.
AMR->YAGO mapping reliability: PMI-based mapping uses a small AMR corpus (~2,756 mentions) to map to thousands of YAGO types; fine-grained type quality and noise rates are uncertain.

Interlanguage link and KB property coverage: variability in cross-lingual link availability and DBpedia/YAGO property density across languages (especially low-resource Wikipedias) is a critical factor whose per-language statistics are not reported.

Translation mining coverage and precision: exhaustive sub-span GIZA++ alignments on short title pairs may be noisy and, importantly, the fraction of mentions that receive useful translations (and the precision of those translations) is not quantified.

End-to-end linking recall and NIL handling: linking accuracy is reported only for "linkable" mentions with surface-form candidates; candidate-generation coverage and NIL/unlinkable rates (which determine real-world utility) are missing.

Self-training robustness across typologies: empirical self-training gains are shown mainly for Turkish; whether seed selection and iterative expansion reliably improve or sometimes amplify noise across many language families remains unclear.
model_diversity_effects: Role specialization of reviewers produced complementary foci: structure_analyst emphasized logical coherence and pipeline dependencies; methodology_auditor stressed reproducibility and missing evaluation metrics; novelty assessors highlighted scale and where components are innovative; claim_verifier aggregated evidence and uncertainty. This diversity surfaced both technical strengths (engineering scale, module-wise plausibility) and evaluation blind spots (silver-test circularity, per-language coverage diagnostics) more clearly than any single perspective would.

Different reviewer priors generated graded risk assessments: reviewers with reproducibility-first priors flagged major flaws around omitted metrics (end-to-end recall, AMR mapping diagnostics), while novelty-focused reviewers were more ready to treat sparse prior art as an innovation signal; preserving both perspectives clarifies that novelty and engineering scale are real but that validity hinges on the underreported diagnostics.

The ensemble of models kept disagreements controlled: no reviewer claimed identical absolute conclusions; instead differences concentrated on severity and remediation urgency — this plurality helps highlight which gaps are methodological necessities versus desirable additional analyses.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Treat the submission as a strong, large-scale engineering/resource contribution that plausibly produces broadly useful silver-standard artifacts, but which currently lacks critical diagnostics needed to evaluate real-world utility across typologies. Key information required before endorsing broad claims: (1) sample-based human evaluation against gold annotations (span, type, link) across a stratified set of languages (include low-, mid-, high-mention Wikipedias; space/no-space scripts; morphologically rich languages), (2) per-language diagnostics reporting interlanguage-link coverage, DBpedia/YAGO property density per entity, fraction of mentions with mined translations, and candidate-generation coverage (fraction of mentions with at least one KB candidate), (3) end-to-end linking metrics including NIL/unlinkable rates and overall precision/recall/F1, (4) diagnostics and precision estimates for AMR->YAGO mappings (e.g., precision@k, sampled spot checks), and (5) broader ablations for self-training and morphology modules across representative languages to demonstrate robustness. If the authors provide these diagnostics and, where necessary, show how to trade coverage for precision (e.g., using confidence thresholds, filtered mappings), the resource and pipeline will be much better substantiated for release and use. Emphasize that the editor's decision should weigh the engineering scale plus any remedial analyses supplied, and that scale is valuable but not sufficient in the absence of per-language quality evidence.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript and substantiate cross-lingual generalization claims, provide the following targeted additions and clarifications: (1) Human-evaluation sample: publish span/type/link gold annotations for a stratified sample (suggest ~20 languages across typologies) and report precision/recall/F1 against these human judgments with inter-annotator agreement. (2) Per-language diagnostics: for all 282 languages or for representative tiers, report counts and distributions for (a) number of propagated labels, (b) fraction of pages with interlanguage links, (c) average number of DBpedia/YAGO properties per entity, (d) number of mined translation pairs and fraction of mentions covered by translation dictionary, and (e) candidate-generation coverage (linkable fraction). (3) AMR->YAGO mapping audit: provide top-k mapping tables, precision estimates from sampling, and an ablation showing downstream typing/linking sensitivity when low-confidence mappings are removed or when only coarser types are used. (4) Linking end-to-end metrics: report coverage (linkable vs unlinkable mentions), NIL detection rates, and overall precision/recall/F1 for linking across languages; include examples of common failure modes. (5) Self-training and morphology ablations: run enable/disable experiments for these modules on a representative language set (including low-mention and space-less scripts) and report whether self-training improves or degrades precision over iterations (precision drift). (6) Reproducibility package: release code, exact KB/Wikipedia dump versions, GIZA++ parameters, AMR and mapping tables, per-language affix lists, sampled intermediate outputs, and the extraction scripts. (7) Clarify thresholds and confidence scoring in the resource release so downstream users can filter for higher precision if desired. Provide these analyses in the main paper or supplementary material and annotate resource files with provenance and confidence scores.
transparency_report: Reported: core algorithmic procedures and many hyperparameters are described (e.g., NPMI seed threshold τ=0, clustering n=20, training selection D=30,000), and per-language silver results (Table 3) are provided at scale.

Missing or underreported items identified by reviewers: (a) per-language KB/link coverage statistics (interlanguage link counts, property counts), (b) AMR->YAGO mapping quality metrics (precision, sample mappings), (c) coverage and precision statistics for mined translation pairs per language, (d) candidate-generation coverage and end-to-end linking recall/NIL rates, (e) sensitivity analyses and ablations for key modules across a representative language sample, (f) complete reproducibility metadata (exact Wikipedia/DBpedia/YAGO/GIZA++ versions and parameter settings).

Suggested transparency improvements for authors to include in revision/supplement: per-language diagnostic tables, sampled human-evaluated annotation subsets with inter-annotator agreement, mapping and lexicon precision estimates via sampling, full reproducibility checklist (data dumps, code, parameters), and annotation provenance/confidence scores embedded in released resources.
epistemic_limits: The reviewers' synthesis is limited by the material provided: most large-scale quantitative claims are evaluated on silver-standard data produced by the same pipeline, so independent validation is limited. We cannot observe the authors' raw intermediate artifacts (AMR->YAGO tables, per-language translation lexica, interlanguage link coverage) unless released; absent those, our judgments about generalizability beyond the reported cases rely on extrapolations from known failure modes of the component methods (alignment noise, propagation errors, seed-noise amplification). Statistical uncertainty remains about per-language performance distributions, mapping precision for thousands of YAGO types derived from a small AMR sample, and end-to-end linking recall because unlinkable/NIL cases are not reported. Consequently, while the engineering scale and within-silver consistency are credible, claims about broad cross-lingual real-world utility require the additional diagnostics and human evaluations requested above to move from plausible to well-supported.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript presents a fully automatic, end-to-end pipeline that mines Wikipedia markups and KB properties (DBpedia/YAGO) to produce large-scale silver-standard name span/type/link annotations and train BiLSTM-CRF taggers plus an unsupervised collective linker for 282 languages. Core steps: AMR->YAGO mapping to obtain multi-granular types; English-page classification using DBpedia/YAGO properties; cross-lingual propagation via interlanguage/redirect links; NPMI-seeded clusterwise self-training; anchor-derived morphology features; exhaustive title-subspan translation mining with GIZA++; and KN-based unsupervised linking scored by salience/similarity/coherence. Empirical evidence includes large-scale silver 70/30 Wikipedia splits (per-language tagging F-scores and linking accuracy, Table 3), morphology and self-training ablations for specific languages (Turkish, Uzbek), and out-of-domain comparisons on nine LORELEI languages showing silver-trained models within ~5.8–17.6% absolute F of gold-supervised models. The pipeline is an engineering-scale resource contribution, but major evaluation and diagnostic gaps limit confident claims about human-gold generalization and end-to-end utility.
strengths: Engineering scale and integration: coherent end-to-end pipeline applied to 282 Wikipedia languages with promise to release silver annotations, morphology analyzers, translation lexica, and models (large resource/benchmark contribution).

Module diversity and pragmatic KB use: combines multiple KB-mining ideas—AMR->YAGO multi-granular typing, DBpedia/YAGO property features, anchor-driven morphology extraction, exhaustive title-subspan translation mining—into a single automated workflow that avoids per-language annotation.

Evidence of measurable module gains: reported substantial morphology gains for Turkish/Uzbek and self-training gains for Turkish; Non-Wikipedia evaluations (nine languages) show silver-trained models can approach supervised models within reported gaps for some languages.
Reuses and adapts established techniques (GIZA++ alignments, NPMI seeding, KN-based linking) in a novel, large-scale configuration to address zero-human multilingual IE.
limitations: Primary evaluation circularity: the large-scale per-language metrics (Table 3) are computed on silver-standard 70/30 splits generated by the same automated pipeline—this risks inflating performance estimates because train and test share the same annotation heuristics and noise rather than measuring agreement with human gold labels.

Incomplete linking coverage metrics: linking accuracy is reported only for 'linkable' mentions (those with surface-form candidates). Candidate-generation coverage, fraction of unlinkable mentions, NIL detection rates and end-to-end linking recall/precision are not reported, obscuring the system's practical utility.

AMR->YAGO mapping fragility: fine-grained type mappings rely on PMI computed from a small AMR corpus (~2,756 mentions). Mapping thousands of YAGO types from such a small sample likely introduces noisy mappings that can propagate systematic type errors across languages.

Unquantified translation/propagation coverage and noise: the title-subspan + GIZA++ translation mining is illustrated with examples but lacks corpus-level statistics (per-language counts, precision/coverage of mined pairs) and the approach crucially depends on interlanguage link coverage, which is not reported per language.
open_questions: Please report sample-based human evaluation against gold annotations (span boundaries, coarse and fine types, and linking) for a stratified set of languages (suggestion: include low/medium/high mention-count Wikipedias, space/no-space scripts, morphologically rich languages). What are precision/recall/F1 and inter-annotator agreement on those samples?

Provide per-language diagnostics: (a) fraction of pages/entities with interlanguage links, (b) average number of DBpedia/YAGO properties per entity, (c) number of propagated labels and mentions per language, (d) fraction of mentions covered by the mined translation lexicon, and (e) fraction of mentions with at least one candidate in candidate generation. How do these correlate with per-language tagging/linking performance?

Give quantitative audit of AMR->YAGO mappings: show top-k mappings, precision estimates from sampling, and an ablation where low-confidence mappings are removed or mapping is limited to coarser types—how sensitive are downstream typing and tagging results to mapping noise?

Report end-to-end linking metrics that include unlinkable mentions and NIL handling (overall precision, recall, F1). Also provide candidate-generation coverage per language and examples of common failure modes (transliteration/inflection mismatches, ambiguous titles).
consensus_snapshot: Reviewers agree the work is a substantial engineering/resource effort that plausibly produces large-scale silver annotations and models across hundreds of languages.
There is broad agreement that the pipeline components are individually plausible and some modules (morphology extraction, self-training) show measurable gains for the languages evaluated.

All reviewers concur that key dependencies (interlanguage link quality, DBpedia/YAGO property density, AMR sample size, translation coverage) are critical and underreported, and that reporting per-language diagnostics and human evaluations is necessary to substantiate broad generalization claims.
disagreement_snapshot: Degree-of-concern severity: some reviewers characterize the silver-test dependence and missing end-to-end linking recall as major methodological flaws needing remediation before asserting broad utility; others treat these gaps as addressable with additional diagnostics and limited supplemental human evaluation.

Novelty emphasis: reviewers differ on whether the contribution is primarily large-scale integration of known methods (incremental) or includes disruptions (AMR->YAGO mapping, anchor-derived morphology, exhaustive title-subspan mining) that should be seen as more novel; all agree scale amplifies impact either way.
uncertainty_snapshot: High uncertainty about how well silver-derived performance translates to human-gold performance across typologies and low-resource languages because most reported metrics are silver-internal and out-of-domain validation is limited to nine languages.
Uncertainty about fine-grained typing quality due to small AMR mapping sample; mapping noise could materially degrade multi-granular type utility.

Uncertain coverage and precision of mined translations and their impact on candidate generation and end-to-end linking, particularly for languages with sparse interlanguage links or non-Latin scripts.

human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: The submission documents an ambitious, integrated pipeline and a large-scale resource claim. Treat it as a substantial engineering/resource contribution that requires additional diagnostic evidence before broad generalization claims are fully supported. Request from authors: (1) sample-based human-evaluated comparisons to gold annotations (spans, coarse/fine types, links) across a stratified set of languages and scripts; (2) per-language diagnostics (interlanguage-link coverage, DBpedia/YAGO property density, translation lexicon size, candidate-generation coverage); (3) AMR->YAGO mapping precision estimates and downstream ablations; (4) end-to-end linking metrics including NIL/unlinkable rates; (5) representative ablations of self-training and morphology across typologies; and (6) reproducibility package with exact KB/Wikipedia dump versions, code, and intermediary artifacts. If these are supplied and show acceptable precision/coverage tradeoffs (or clear provenance/confidence metadata enabling downstream filtering), the work stands as a valuable large-scale resource. Without these diagnostics, claims about broad real-world utility should be tempered.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen claims and resource usability, please provide: (1) Human-evaluation: gold annotations (spans/types/links) on a stratified sample of languages (recommend ~20 diverse languages) and report precision/recall/F1 with inter-annotator agreement. (2) Per-language diagnostics: tables or summary stats for interlanguage-link coverage, average DBpedia/YAGO property counts per entity, number of propagated labels, count and coverage of mined translation pairs, and fraction of mentions with candidate entities. (3) AMR->YAGO audit: top-k mappings, sampled precision estimates, and an ablation showing downstream sensitivity to filtering low-confidence mappings. (4) Linking end-to-end metrics: candidate-generation coverage, fraction linkable vs unlinkable, NIL assignment rates, and overall linking precision/recall/F1 with qualitative error examples. (5) Robustness ablations: enable/disable self-training and morphology modules across representative languages (including space-less scripts and low-mention Wikipedias) and report precision drift across self-training iterations. (6) Reproducibility materials: code, parameter settings, KB/Wikipedia dump versions, per-language affix lists and translation lexica, and provenance/confidence fields in released annotations. (7) If full-scale diagnostics for all 282 languages are infeasible, provide a clear stratified sampling strategy and release sampled per-language artifacts and human-evaluated subsets so downstream users can judge applicability.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: The paper presents a comprehensive, fully automatic pipeline that mines Wikipedia and KB signals to produce silver-standard span/type/link annotations and train taggers/linkers for 282 languages. The integration of AMR->YAGO typing, DBpedia/YAGO property-based classification, cross-lingual propagation, NPMI-seeded self-training, anchor-derived morphology, exhaustive title-subspan translation mining, and KN-based unsupervised linking is an ambitious engineering contribution with promising module-level evidence.

Strengths: Engineering scale and resource potential (282 languages), novel/practical uses of KB features and anchor signals, measurable module gains (morphology, self-training), and pragmatic adaptation of established methods for zero-human multilingual IE.

Limitations: (1) Large-scale evaluation is primarily on silver-standard 70/30 splits derived from the pipeline itself—this introduces circular validation risk and may inflate performance relative to human gold. (2) Linking results exclude unlinkable mentions and NIL handling; end-to-end recall and candidate-generation coverage are unreported. (3) AMR->YAGO fine-grained mappings are based on a small AMR sample (~2,756 mentions) likely yielding noisy mappings that propagate errors. (4) Translation mining and interlanguage-link coverage are not quantified per language; coverage/noise could be severe in low-resource Wikipedias.

Open Questions: (1) Provide stratified human-evaluation (spans/types/links) across diverse languages and report metrics with inter-annotator agreement. (2) Publish per-language diagnostics (interlanguage links, KB property counts, propagated label counts, translation lexicon sizes, candidate-generation coverage) and correlate these with performance. (3) Share AMR->YAGO mapping tables and sampled precision estimates and show downstream sensitivity when low-confidence mappings are filtered. (4) Report end-to-end linking metrics including unlinkable/NIL rates and qualitative failure examples.

Transparency: The manuscript documents many procedures and hyperparameters (NPMI τ, clustering n, training selection), and includes large per-language tables. Missing items that hinder assessing generalization: per-language KB/link coverage stats, AMR->YAGO mapping diagnostics, translation-pair coverage/precision, candidate-generation coverage and NIL rates, broader ablations across typologies, and full reproducibility metadata (dump versions, GIZA++ params, code). Authors should release sampled human-evaluated subsets, per-language artifacts, and provenance/confidence fields to enable downstream filtering and benchmarking.

Overall: The work is a meaningful engineering and resource-scale contribution with important innovations in operationalizing KB signals for zero-human multilingual IE. To substantiate broad generalization claims and maximize resource value, the authors should supply the targeted diagnostics, human-evaluated samples, end-to-end linking coverage metrics, AMR mapping audits, and reproducibility materials requested above.

confidence_interval.rationale: Upper bound reflects credible within-pipeline evidence: detailed methods, per-language silver results, and selective ablations support that the system can reproduce its automated annotations and achieve high silver-domain predictability. Lower bound reflects substantial uncertainties: heavy reliance on silver-only large-scale evaluation, small AMR mapping sample for fine-grained typing, missing per-language KB/link coverage diagnostics, unreported translation coverage and end-to-end linking recall (NIL handling). These gaps could materially reduce practical utility in under-covered or typologically different languages, hence the wide interval.

These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review.
